paras.t: For most of the twentieth century, city planners designed for cars. Wide roads, large car parks and separate zones for housing, shopping and work made sense when petrol was cheap and traffic was light. Over time, however, this approach produced neighbourhoods in which even a loaf of bread required a drive. Today, a growing number of cities are reversing that logic and trying to bring daily destinations within walking distance of people's homes.

The idea is often summarised as the "fifteen-minute city": shops, schools, clinics and parks should be reachable on foot or by bicycle in a quarter of an hour. Supporters argue that this is not a new invention but a return to the way towns grew before mass car ownership. Critics reply that no planning slogan can fit every place, and that people also travel across a city for work, specialised health care and leisure, journeys that no single neighbourhood can absorb.

The health case for walkable districts is straightforward. People who walk or cycle to everyday destinations build physical activity into their routine without needing a gym membership. Doctors point out that this kind of gentle, regular movement is easier to sustain than intensive exercise programmes, which many adults abandon within months. Less traffic also means cleaner air and quieter streets, benefits that are felt most strongly by children and older residents.

Local shops have a stake in the change as well. Studies of streets that were closed to cars on a trial basis often report that customers visit more often, although they tend to spend less on each visit. Shop owners are frequently suspicious at first, fearing that drivers will go elsewhere. In several cases those fears faded once the owners saw the number of passers-by rise, but the evidence is not uniform, and some businesses that depend on deliveries have struggled.

Not everyone gains equally. Neighbourhoods that become pleasant to walk in tend to become more expensive, and long-standing residents may be priced out. Planners therefore combine street improvements with measures to keep housing affordable, such as limits on rent increases or requirements that new developments include lower-cost flats. Without such measures, the people the policy is meant to help may be the first to leave.

Finally, there is the question of speed. Redesigning a street can take a few weeks with paint and planters, but rebuilding a district's shops, schools and homes takes decades. Most experts therefore see walkable planning as a direction rather than a destination: small changes made consistently, rather than a single dramatic transformation.

paras.t: Adaptive learning software, which adjusts the difficulty of exercises according to a student's answers, is no longer experimental. Schools in many countries now use it for mathematics and language practice, and a newer generation of tools built on large language models can hold a written conversation with a learner, explaining a mistake in several different ways until one of them makes sense.

The appeal is easy to see. A teacher with thirty pupils cannot sit beside each one while they struggle with a problem; software can. Pupils who are ahead can move on without waiting, and those who are behind can repeat a topic without feeling embarrassed in front of classmates. Several teachers interviewed for this article said that their most anxious pupils were the ones who gained most from this private practice.

Yet the technology has limits that its enthusiasts sometimes underplay. Software is good at checking whether an answer is right, but much less reliable at judging whether an argument is well reasoned or an essay original. Language models can also produce confident explanations that are wrong, which is a particular risk for learners who are not yet able to tell the difference. For this reason, most educators advise treating such tools as a first draft of help rather than an authority.

A further concern is attention. Tools that reward quick answers can encourage pupils to guess and move on, and some researchers warn that the effort of struggling with a problem is itself part of learning. If a program removes every difficulty, they argue, it may also remove the benefit. Designers respond by building in pauses and asking pupils to explain their thinking before showing a solution, though how well these features work is still being studied.

What, then, is the role of the teacher? The most common view among those interviewed was that the teacher's job shifts rather than shrinks. With routine practice handled by software, teachers can spend more time on discussion, on projects and on pupils who need personal encouragement. A few, however, feared that schools under financial pressure might treat the software as a cheaper replacement for staff instead of a support for them.

paras.t: Parents of teenagers often complain that their children cannot get up in the morning. For a long time this was put down to laziness or too much time on screens. Sleep researchers now offer a more biological explanation: during adolescence the internal body clock shifts, so that teenagers naturally feel sleepy later in the evening and wake later in the morning than children or older adults.

This shift is thought to be driven partly by changes in the timing of melatonin, a hormone that helps the body prepare for sleep. In teenagers, melatonin rises later at night than in younger children. As a result, a teenager asked to fall asleep at ten o'clock may simply not feel tired, however hard they try, and may lie awake for an hour or more.

The problem is made worse by school timetables. In many countries lessons begin at around eight o'clock or earlier, which means pupils must wake at a time when their bodies are still biologically 'at night'. Surveys regularly show that many teenagers sleep less than the eight to ten hours that health authorities recommend, and the shortfall tends to build up over the school week.

Lack of sleep affects more than mood. Tired pupils find it harder to concentrate and to remember new material, and some studies link persistent sleep shortage with a higher risk of accidents and of low mood. Teachers also report that the first lessons of the day can be unproductive, with pupils present in the classroom but only partly alert.

Several schools and districts have experimented with later start times. Results have varied, but a number of reports describe improved attendance and fewer pupils falling asleep in class. Not all families welcome the change: later finishes can clash with sports training, part-time jobs and childcare duties, and some parents say that evenings become shorter rather than mornings longer.

Researchers are cautious about drawing firm conclusions. Sleep is hard to measure outside a laboratory, and it is affected by diet, stress, family routines and the use of devices at night. Most agree, however, that expecting teenagers to behave like early risers is unrealistic, and that schools and parents should at least be aware of the biology involved.
